Let’s talk about something that’s often left unspoken, but really matters: why honest conversations about death matter.
For a lot of people, just hearing the word “death” is enough to make them uncomfortable. It’s a topic many of us would rather sidestep—maybe it feels too heavy, or just plain scary. But here’s the thing: the more we talk about it openly, the less it controls us. When we have real conversations about death, especially with kids, fear can actually turn into curiosity. And uncertainty? That can shift into understanding.
I remember a parent sharing how tough it was to explain the loss of a grandparent to her young son. She worried she’d say the wrong thing, or maybe scare him. But when she finally sat down with him, his questions were so honest and simple. Things like, “Where did Grandpa go?” and “Will he come back?” She answered as truthfully as she could, and you know what? Her son, satisfied, just went right back to playing. That tough conversation actually brought them both a sense of relief.
What’s surprising is that children are often much more resilient than we expect. Their questions might catch us off guard, but they’re just trying to make sense of the world. When we respond with honesty and openness, we teach them that death is a part of life—not some dark secret to be feared or hidden away.
In my work, I’ve seen firsthand that families who talk about death ahead of time are often better prepared when loss happens. They don’t get blindsided by the details, and they’re able to make choices that really reflect what matters most to them. On the other hand, families who avoid the subject? They’re usually the ones left feeling overwhelmed and unprepared when the time comes.
There’s a movement growing called “death positivity.” It’s not about being morbid—it’s about facing the reality that death is a natural part of life. By breaking the silence, we give ourselves the chance to confront our fears, and maybe even find new meaning in the face of mortality.
I’ve led workshops and community events where anyone can come and ask questions—no judgment, just honest conversation. Sometimes people want to know things like, “How long does it take for a body to decompose?” Other times, they ask, “What happens after we die?” These talks can be serious, sure, but there’s often laughter, too. And always, there’s honesty.
What I’ve noticed is this: the more you know, the less there is to fear. When we shine a light on the unknown, myths and taboos lose their grip. Even the hardest questions can be answered—with compassion, with clarity, and with kindness.
